title: Xcel Energy undergrounding power lines in Palo Duro Canyon State Park to help wildfire mitigation

body_markdown:
**CANYON, Texas** (Nov. 18, 2026) — Xcel Energy is burying selected power lines in Palo Duro Canyon State Park to help reduce the risk of wildfire ignition, while enhancing the view of the canyon. Crews are undergrounding these overhead distribution facilities on state park property, inside of the canyon and at the top, from the TxDOT right-of-way.


“This is a transformative project for the park and the visitors we serve. Moving utilities underground improves safety for visitors and staff, strengthens our wildfire mitigation efforts, and protects the viewshed for future generations,” said David Fischer, Park Superintendent. “We appreciate Xcel Energy’s partnership and investment in helping preserve the safety and beauty of Palo Duro Canyon State Park.”


This targeted undergrounding project is split between more than 10 phases and includes primary and secondary facilities to help mitigate against ignitions from overhead utility lines. More than six miles of overhead 15kV powerlines will be removed, and crews will install 3-phase primary lines underground, along with secondary lines to meters.


The project will take place across both Randall and Armstrong Counties, totaling 7.31 line miles placed underground once work is completed in June of 2027. Xcel Energy’s line crews in Canyon, Texas are performing utility work, and Driver Directional is the contractor on the project.


Archaeological and geological analyses were performed with permits from the Texas Parks and Wildlife Department before the project started to ensure there were no sites that would require work to stop or be re-routed.


Xcel Energy is grateful for the partnership and cooperation of TPWD as crews continue to bury lines. In the future, this project will benefit Palo Duro Canyon State Park with a force water main installation.


As an added benefit, less vegetation management, such as trimming trees and bushes, will be required near the roadway after overhead lines are removed.


“Not every line should be buried, so we are only doing this where it makes sense,” said Eran Moore, director of distribution design, Xcel Energy. “There are several benefits to burying targeted lines where the fire risk is high. Putting power lines underground takes certain hazards out of the equation, like overhead exposure, high winds and vegetation that can catch a spark.”


It is not possible or cost-effective to underground all power lines. Where overhead lines remain, mitigation efforts can include: fire-resistant equipment, electrical protection devices and inspection of lines and poles.


These efforts help make Xcel Energy’s electric system more resilient during severe weather. The company uses multiple layers of protection to help reduce wildfire risk.


“There is no single solution to the threat that wildfire poses, but burying lines in certain high-risk areas helps reduce risk,” said Wes Reeves, senior wildfire community engagement manager, Xcel Energy. “Our approach is to match the right solution to the right location and continually evolve how we prepare for and respond to fire-weather conditions.”


Other Xcel Energy targeted undergrounding projects in the Texas Panhandle include work around Timber Creek Canyon, River Falls, Sunday Canyon and the Palo Duro Club.
